content.value:
Your starter file contains a complete PID turn-to-heading controller. The code is already wired — P, I, D, angle wrapping, and motor output.

It starts with kP=0.02 and target heading set to 90 degrees. The robot will turn right immediately when you press START.

It uses CommandOpMode with MotorEx wrappers for all four drive motors. D-pad left/right are bound via GamepadButton.whenPressed() to shift the target by 90 degrees.

Run it now. The robot should turn to face 90 degrees and stop.

Your job is not to write the PID code — it's to understand how each part works, then tune the constants.

Find this line:

double power = kP * error + kI * integral + kD * derivative;

The P term is kP * error. It produces output proportional to how far off you are.

At 90 degrees of error with kP=0.1: power = 0.1 * 90 = 9.0 (motor caps at 1.0).

At 5 degrees: power = 0.1 * 5 = 0.5 (gentle correction as you approach).

The motor's setPower() clamps to [-1.0, 1.0] internally, so no explicit clamp is needed.

Try tuning: increase kP. Higher kP means faster turns but more overshoot. Find the value where the robot oscillates, then back off to ~70% of that.

steps.title: I: Integral — fixes the last few degrees

content.value:
Find these lines:

integral += error;
if (Math.signum(error) != Math.signum(prevError)) { integral = 0; }

The I term is kI * integral. It accumulates error over time.

If the robot is stuck at 2 degrees, P alone (0.01 * 2 = 0.02) may be too weak to overcome friction. The integral builds up: 2 + 2 + 2 + ... until the accumulated correction is large enough to push through.

The signum check is the windup guard. When error crosses zero (we overshot), the integral resets. This prevents the accumulated error from fighting against our correction on the other side.

Try tuning: set kI to 0.001. Watch the robot eliminate that last 1-2 degrees of steady-state error.

Find these lines:

double derivative = error - prevError;
prevError = error;

The D term is kD * derivative. It measures how fast the error is changing.

When the robot approaches the target quickly, error shrinks fast, making derivative negative. This subtracts from the output — a braking force proportional to approach speed.

prevError is saved BEFORE the new error is computed. derivative = currentError - previousError tells us the rate of change between ticks.

Try tuning: set kD to 0.001. Increase it until the robot approaches smoothly without bouncing. Too much D will make the approach sluggish.

Now tune the full controller:

1. Set kI = 0 and kD = 0. Increase kP until the robot oscillates around the target, then set kP to ~70% of that value.

2. Increase kD until overshoot disappears and the robot settles cleanly without bouncing.

3. Increase kI just enough to eliminate any remaining steady-state error.

The robot should settle within 2 degrees of target in under 1.5 seconds. Try different targets with d-pad to verify.

This is the same PID architecture that SolversLib's PIDController uses internally. setVeloCoefficients(kP, kI, kD) on a Motor configures exactly these three terms.
